title: Reactive and Rendering Optimization
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of Reactive and Rendering Optimization in a Vue 3 application.
Apply at least one of the syllabus subtopics in a small, inspectable example.
Verify one expected behavior and identify a relevant edge case.

content.intro: This lesson studies Reactive and Rendering Optimization within Performance and Optimization. The source PDF subtopics are preserved below and connected to an original working-style example.
content.why_it_matters: Profiling avoids guesswork and helps developers optimize the bottleneck that users actually experience.

content_blocks.title: Reactive and Rendering Optimization: Measure before optimizing
content_blocks.alt_text: Measure before optimizing diagram for lesson 131: Reactive and Rendering Optimization. Record the same route, data, and device → Identify the actual render or bundle bottleneck → Repeat measurements and check behavior
content_blocks.caption: Performance workflow: measure a reproducible baseline, optimize the observed bottleneck, and repeat the same test.

content_blocks.title: The idea in context
content_blocks.text: Vue performance work starts with measurement and distinguishes initial load costs from reactive update costs. This lesson focuses on Reactive and Rendering Optimization. Start by naming the state, component, browser behavior, or deployment boundary involved; then predict what should change and test the smallest example.

items.title: Avoiding unnecessary reactive state
items.text: For Avoiding unnecessary reactive state, identify the reactive source that changes and the value or side effect that depends on it. Prefer computed values for derived data; use watchers when a change must trigger work outside pure derivation, and keep dependencies explicit.

items.title: Using computed properties effectively
items.text: For Using computed properties effectively, identify the reactive source that changes and the value or side effect that depends on it. Prefer computed values for derived data; use watchers when a change must trigger work outside pure derivation, and keep dependencies explicit.

items.title: Keeping component boundaries appropriate
items.text: For Keeping component boundaries appropriate, document what data enters the component, which events leave it, and where shared content or behavior belongs. Keep props one-way, emit changes rather than mutating parent-owned values, and add slots only when a real composition point is needed.

items.title: Avoiding unnecessary watchers
items.text: For Avoiding unnecessary watchers, identify the reactive source that changes and the value or side effect that depends on it. Prefer computed values for derived data; use watchers when a change must trigger work outside pure derivation, and keep dependencies explicit.

items.title: Handling large lists efficiently
items.text: For Handling large lists efficiently, connect the term to a visible behavior in a small Vue 3 example. State what input or reactive dependency changes, predict the UI result, and verify the prediction with a normal case plus a boundary case.

content_blocks.expected_output: Typing filters the two rows; the result is derived instead of stored as a second mutable list.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run as App.vue. For very large datasets, measure and consider server filtering or a maintained virtualization component.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the initial values or original code, reload the development app/test, and repeat once with a boundary or failure case. Remove temporary logs and test data before committing.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Work through Reactive and Rendering Optimization with a predict–change–verify loop. First state the expected UI or console output. Change only the relevant input/state value, then observe the result. Compare it with the expected output in the code block; if it differs, check the exact file, runtime/version, browser Console, and network response before widening the investigation.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Extend the example to include “Using computed properties effectively”. Keep the same behavior for the ordinary input, then try an empty, invalid, repeated, or failure condition that makes sense for the example. Record the expected result before testing.

items.title: Assuming behavior instead of checking it
items.text: Write down the expected result and reproduce the issue in the smallest possible example; inspect the browser Console and the exact reactive value or request.

items.title: Ignoring an edge case
items.text: Try empty input, a missing item, repeated interaction, a failed request, or unmounting while work is pending; handle the case explicitly.

items.title: Putting every responsibility in one component
items.text: Separate display, reusable logic, API service, and shared state when that boundary makes the behavior easier to test and explain.

content_blocks.text: Remember: Vue performance work starts with measurement and distinguishes initial load costs from reactive update costs. content_blocks.title: Accessibility, version, and runtime notes
content_blocks.text: Use semantic HTML, readable labels, keyboard-operable controls, and visible errors where the example interacts with users. Vue examples are intended for Vue 3.x with create-vue/Vite unless a legacy or specialist lesson explicitly says otherwise. This CodeLeaf playground does not execute arbitrary Vue code; the snippets are labeled for static validation and should be run in a separate local project.

content.task: Create a small example for “Reactive and Rendering Optimization” that applies “Avoiding unnecessary reactive state”, predicts the expected result, and verifies a relevant boundary case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates the named Vue concept rather than only mentioning it.
The expected output or observable behavior is written down and can be checked locally.
At least one boundary, loading, invalid-input, or failure case is tested or explicitly reasoned about.
The example uses semantic/accessible interaction patterns and does not treat frontend state as authoritative security.
hints: Start with the smallest observable part of “Avoiding unnecessary reactive state”.
Predict the output before changing one input at a time.
Use the browser Console, Vue DevTools, or the appropriate test runner to isolate a mismatch.

common_mistakes.problem: The example only covers the happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Real interfaces receive empty values, delayed responses, invalid input, and failed requests.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one realistic edge/failure case and state its expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: The code assumes an API or feature exists in every runtime.
common_mistakes.why: Tool and API support depends on Vue, the build tool, or the chosen SSR/test framework.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the linked official reference and record the runtime/version assumption.

summary: Reactive and Rendering Optimization belongs to the broader area Performance and Optimization.
The main concept to practice is Avoiding unnecessary reactive state.
Verify a normal result and one meaningful boundary case before using the pattern in a production feature.
